questions.question:
Study the HTTP request-response flow below:

Client → DNS Lookup → IP Resolved → TCP Handshake → HTTP GET /index.html → Server → 301 Moved Permanently → Client → HTTP GET /index.html (HTTPS) → 200 OK

At which step does the browser first establish a secure encrypted channel?

values: Step 2: Server responds 301 Moved Permanently → Location: https://...
Step 4: TLS Handshake complete — encrypted channel established
Step 6: Server responds 200 OK over encrypted channel

options: Step 1 — HTTP GET already uses encryption
Step 3 — TLS Handshake initiates the secure channel
Step 2 — 301 redirect triggers immediate encryption
Step 5 — Only after sending HTTPS GET is encryption active
questions.answer: Step 3 — TLS Handshake initiates the secure channel

questions.question:
A browser sends this request:

GET /api/users HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Connection: keep-alive
If-None-Match: "abc123"

The server responds with HTTP 304. What does the browser do next?
options: Displays an error page — 304 means the resource is unavailable
Re-requests the resource with a POST method
Uses its locally cached copy of the resource — 304 Not Modified means the cache is still valid
Clears the cache and fetches the resource fresh
questions.answer: Uses its locally cached copy of the resource — 304 Not Modified means the cache is still valid

questions.question: HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2.0 — which statement CORRECTLY describes an advantage of HTTP/2.0?
options: HTTP/2.0 requires HTTPS; HTTP/1.1 works over both HTTP and HTTPS
HTTP/2.0 uses multiplexing — multiple requests can be sent over a single TCP connection simultaneously, eliminating head-of-line blocking
HTTP/2.0 replaces TCP with UDP for faster connections
HTTP/2.0 supports only binary data; HTTP/1.1 supports text and binary
questions.answer: HTTP/2.0 uses multiplexing — multiple requests can be sent over a single TCP connection simultaneously, eliminating head-of-line blocking

questions.question:
Scenario:
An e-commerce site uses stateless HTTP. After login, a user adds items to a cart across multiple pages. Which mechanism is MOST appropriate for maintaining session state across these stateless requests?
options: Using HTTP PUT method to store state on the server per request
Using a session cookie or token (e.g., JWT) sent with each request so the server can identify the user
Upgrading to HTTP/2.0 which supports stateful connections
Storing session data in the HTTP request headers directly
questions.answer: Using a session cookie or token (e.g., JWT) sent with each request so the server can identify the user

questions.question: A developer notices their API returns HTTP 401 for one endpoint and HTTP 403 for another. What is the semantic difference?

401 means resource not found; 403 means method not allowed

questions.answer: 401 Unauthorized means the request lacks valid authentication credentials; 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but denies access

questions.question: What is the key difference between the HTML attributes 'defer' and 'async' on a <script> tag?

async is for internal scripts; defer is for external scripts
